    AI Overview
    An orbit is a regular, repeating gravitational path of an object, such as a planet, moon, or satellite, around a central body. It is a curved trajectory—typically elliptical—governed by the balance between an object’s velocity and the force of gravity. Key types include low Earth orbit (LEO), geostationary orbit (GEO), and polar orbit. 
    Key Characteristics and Components 
    • Definition: The path of an object in space around another, or a set of points in a dynamical system.
    • Shape:
      Most orbits are elliptical (oval), though they can be perfectly circular or parabolic.
    • Components: Key elements include the central body, the orbiting object (satellite), and the force of gravity.
    • Speed: Objects must move at a specific velocity, known as orbital velocity, to maintain their path without falling back or flying away.
    • Perigee/Periapsis: The point in an orbit closest to the body being orbited.
    • Apogee/Apoapsis: The point in an orbit farthest from the body being orbited. 
    Types of Orbits 
    • Low Earth Orbit (LEO): Close to Earth (160 to 2,000 km altitude), typically used for space stations and satellites.
    • Geostationary Orbit (GEO): A circular orbit 35,786 km above Earth's equator, allowing satellites to stay over the same spot.
    • Polar Orbit: An orbit that passes over or near both poles.
    • Sun-Synchronous Orbit: A nearly polar orbit that passes over any given spot on Earth's surface at the same local solar time. 
    How Orbit is Calculated & Key Equations
    Orbits are calculated using celestial mechanics, often relying on Newton's law of universal gravitation and Kepler's laws of planetary motion. 
    • Gravity Equation:
      (Force equals gravitational constant times the two masses divided by the distance squared).
    • Orbital Velocity:
      (Velocity equals the square root of the gravitational constant times the central mass divided by the radius).       
    History of the Concept 
    • Ancient Views: Early astronomers believed in geocentric models where everything orbited the Earth.
    • Copernican Revolution: Nicolaus Copernicus proposed a heliocentric (sun-centered) model.
    • Kepler and Newton: Johannes Kepler determined that orbits were elliptical (not perfectly circular), and Isaac Newton later developed the physical laws explaining why objects orbit.
    • Space Age: In 1962, John Glenn became the first American to enter Earth orbit. 
    Common Uses 
    • Satellites: Telecommunications, navigation (GPS), weather monitoring, and scientific research.
    • Space Exploration: International Space Station (ISS), lunar missions.
    • Physics: In atomic models, electrons orbit the nucleus.

      What is an Orbit in Physics? Definition: An orbit is the curved path followed by an object under the influence of gravity as it moves around a larger body, such as a planet around the Sun or a satellite around Earth. Explanation: Orbits occur because of a balance between forward motion and gravitational pull: • Gravity pulls the object inward. • Forward velocity keeps it moving sideways. • The result is continuous free fall around the central body, instead of crashing into it. Types of Orbits: • Circular orbit → constant distance from centre. • Elliptical orbit → varying distance, with closest point = perihelion/perigee and farthest = aphelion/apogee. • Geostationary orbit → satellite appears fixed over one spot on Earth (24-hour period). Imagine: Think of swinging a stone tied to a string. The string pulls the stone inward (like gravity), while the stone’s speed keeps it moving in a circle, that’s how orbits work. In simple terms: An orbit is the path an object takes when it keeps “falling around” another object due to gravity. Formula (Orbital Velocity): v = √(GM/R) Where: • G = gravitational constant • M = mass of central body • R = distance

    Definitions from Oxford Languages · Learn more
    or·bit
    /ˈôrbət/
    Learn to pronounce
    noun
    noun: orbit; plural noun: orbits
    1. 1.
      the curved path of a celestial object or spacecraft around a star, planet, or moon, especially a periodic elliptical revolution.
      "the Earth's orbit around the sun"
      h
      Similar:
      course
      path
      circuit
      track
      trajectory
      rotation
      revolution
      circle
      cycle
      round
      circumgyration
      • one complete circuit around an orbited body.
        "the satellite will complete one orbit every 12 hours"
      • the state of being on or moving in an orbit.
        "planets in orbit around the sun"
      • the path of an electron around an atomic nucleus.
    2. 2.
      a sphere of activity, interest, or application.
      "a radical filmmaker outside the Hollywood orbit"
      h
      Similar:
      sphere
      sphere of influence
      area of activity
      range
      reach
      scope
      ambit
      compass
      sweep
      jurisdiction
      authority
      remit
      span of control
      domain
      realm
      province
      territory
      preserve
      department
      turf
      bailiwick
    3. 3.
      Anatomy
      the cavity in the skull of a vertebrate that contains the eye; the eye socket.
      • the area around the eye of a bird or other animal.
    verb
    verb: orbit; 3rd person present: orbits; past tense: orbited; past participle: orbited; gerund or present participle: orbiting
    1. (of a celestial object or spacecraft) move in orbit around (a star or planet).
      "Mercury orbits the Sun"
      • fly or move around in a circle.
        "the mobile's disks spun and orbited slowly"
        h
        Similar:
        revolve round
        circle around
        go around
        travel around
        encircle
      • put (a satellite) into orbit.
        "France has been orbiting satellites with her own launcher"
    Phrases
    into orbit — into a state of heightened performance, activity, anger, or excitement.
    "his goal sent the fans into orbit"
    Origin
    late Middle English (in orbit (sense 3 of the noun)): partly via French from Latin orbita ‘course, track’ (in medieval Latin‘eye socket’), feminine of orbitus ‘circular’, from orbis ‘circle, sphere’.
    into orbit
    phrase of orbit
    1. informal
      into a state of heightened performance, activity, anger, or excitement.
      "his goal sent the fans into orbit"
    Use over time for: orbit

    What is the synonym of orbit?
    Some common synonyms of orbit are compass, gamut, range, scope, and sweep. While all these words mean "the extent that lies within the powers of something (as to cover or control)," orbit suggests an often circumscribed range of activity or influence within which forces work toward accommodation.
